title: Current and voltage — the basics of every circuit
examTip: Questions using Q = It, V = W/Q and R = V/I come up almost every year. I-V characteristics are a favourite for 'describe and explain' questions, especially the filament lamp and diode. Examiners want the physics reason, not just the shape.
introTips: This covers electric current, potential difference and resistance. These are the three quantities used in every electricity question
You will practise rearranging Q = It, V = W/Q and R = V/I to find any unknown
By the end, you will be able to sketch and explain I-V graphs for three different components. You will also be able to describe the required practical
intro: Every electrical device you have used works because charge flows around a circuit and transfers energy. That includes your phone, a kettle and Christmas lights. Current, voltage and resistance let you predict exactly how any circuit will behave. Those three ideas come up on almost every electricity paper. Get them right, and a big chunk of Topic 2 becomes simple.

keyPoints.heading: Electric current — charge on the move
keyPoints.content: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge. Charge is measured in coulombs (C) and current in amperes (A). The equation linking them is Q = It. Here Q is charge (C), I is current (A) and t is time (s). So 1 ampere means 1 coulomb of charge passes a point every second. In a metal, it is free electrons that really move. They flow from the negative terminal to the positive terminal. Conventional current goes the opposite way, from positive to negative. This is just a historical habit. Scientists chose the direction before they discovered electrons, and got it the wrong way round. But it is the direction shown on all circuit diagrams, so use it.
writeBullets: Electric current — the rate of flow of charge (coulombs per second)
Ampere (A) — the unit of current. 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹
Q = It — charge (C) = current (A) × time (s)
Free electrons — the charge carriers in metals. They move negative → positive
Conventional current — flows positive → negative (opposite to electron flow)
Ammeter — measures current. Always connected in series

keyTerms.def: Rate of flow of electric charge, measured in amperes (A)
The unit of electric charge (C); 1 coulomb = 1 ampere × 1 second
The direction current is drawn in circuit diagrams — from + to −, opposite to electron flow

keyPoints.memTip: Q = It: 'Quiet Is Time'. Charge = current × time.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Conventional current and electron flow catch people out every year. In a metal, electrons move from − to +. Conventional current goes from + to −. In circuit diagrams, always use the conventional current direction.

keyPoints.heading: Potential difference — the energy push
keyPoints.content: Potential difference (p.d.) is also called voltage. It is the energy transferred per unit of charge as charges move between two points. The equation is V = W/Q. Here V is voltage (volts, V), W is energy (joules, J) and Q is charge (coulombs, C). A p.d. of 1 volt means 1 joule of energy is transferred for every 1 coulomb of charge that passes. The electromotive force (EMF) of a battery is the energy it gives to each coulomb of charge. It is measured in volts too. But the terminal p.d. is slightly less than the EMF. This is the voltage you really measure across the battery terminals in a circuit. It is lower because some energy is 'lost' pushing charge through the battery's own internal resistance. You will meet internal resistance in more detail later. For now, know that terminal p.d. < EMF.
writeBullets: Potential difference (p.d.) — energy transferred per unit charge. Measured in volts (V)
V = W/Q — voltage (V) = energy (J) ÷ charge (C)
1 volt — 1 joule of energy per 1 coulomb of charge
EMF — the energy per unit charge given to charge by the source (for example, a battery)
Terminal p.d. — voltage across the battery terminals in a working circuit. It is less than the EMF because of internal resistance
Voltmeter — measures p.d. Always connected in parallel

keyTerms.def: Energy transferred per coulomb of charge between two points; measured in volts (V)
Energy given to each coulomb of charge by a source such as a battery; measured in volts
The p.d. measured across the battery terminals in a working circuit — always less than EMF

keyPoints.memTip: V = W/Q: 'Voltage is Watts per Queue'. Energy ÷ charge.
keyPoints.tutor_note: EMF and voltage are easy to mix up. EMF is what the battery gives per coulomb. Terminal p.d. is what is really available to the outside circuit. They differ because of internal resistance.

keyPoints.heading: Resistance — the opposition to current
keyPoints.content: Resistance is the opposition to the flow of current. The greater the resistance, the less current flows for a given voltage. The equation linking the three is R = V/I, often called Ohm's law. Here R is resistance in ohms (Ω), V is potential difference in volts, and I is current in amperes. For example, say the p.d. across a resistor is 12 V and the current through it is 3 A. Then R = 12/3 = 4 Ω. Or if V = 12 V and R = 4 Ω, then I = V/R = 12/4 = 3 A. Several factors affect resistance: - length: a longer wire → higher resistance - cross-sectional area: a thicker wire → lower resistance - material: different metals have different resistivities - temperature: for most metals, hotter → higher resistance. The ions vibrate more and get in the way of electron flow
writeBullets: Resistance — opposition to current. Measured in ohms (Ω)
R = V/I — resistance = voltage ÷ current. It rearranges to V = IR and I = V/R
Ohm's law — for an ohmic conductor, R is constant (V ∝ I at constant temperature)
Length — longer wire → greater resistance
Cross-sectional area — thicker wire → lower resistance
Temperature — hotter metal → higher resistance (ions vibrate more and get in the way of electrons)

keyTerms.def: Opposition to the flow of electric current; measured in ohms (Ω)
The unit of resistance; 1 Ω = 1 V A⁻¹
For an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, current is proportional to potential difference

keyPoints.memTip: R = V/I: use the triangle. Put V on top, and I and R on the bottom. Cover any one to get the formula.
keyPoints.tutor_note: In calculations, always write the formula first. Then substitute values, then calculate. Showing your working gets method marks, even if your arithmetic slips.

keyPoints.heading: I-V characteristics — how components really behave
keyPoints.content: An I-V characteristic graph shows how current changes with potential difference for a component. Current (I) goes on the y-axis and potential difference (V) on the x-axis. An ohmic conductor (for example, a fixed resistor at constant temperature) gives a straight line through the origin. Doubling V doubles I, so resistance is constant. A filament lamp gives a curve that flattens as V increases. As the current rises, the filament heats up and its resistance increases. So the graph curves away from the straight line. A diode only lets current flow in one direction (forward bias). In reverse bias, resistance is extremely high and current is almost zero. The forward bias threshold is roughly 0.7 V for a silicon diode. You need to know the shape AND the reason for it. Examiners will ask you to explain, not just describe.
writeBullets: I-V graph — current (y-axis) vs potential difference (x-axis) for a component
Ohmic conductor — straight line through the origin. Resistance is constant
Filament lamp — S-shaped curve. Resistance increases as temperature rises
Diode — conducts in one direction only. Near-zero current in reverse bias
Forward bias threshold — ~0.7 V for a silicon diode, before much current flows
Resistance from an I-V graph — find the gradient (I/V) and take its reciprocal. Or read off V and I and use R = V/I

keyTerms.def: A graph of current against potential difference showing how a component behaves
A component whose resistance stays constant — gives a straight-line I-V graph
A component that allows current in one direction only; very high resistance in reverse

keyPoints.memTip: Three shapes: straight line = resistor. Bendy S = lamp (it gets hot). One-sided hockey stick = diode (one direction only). Cover your notes and sketch all three graphs with labels from memory.
keyPoints.tutor_note: A very common mistake is drawing the filament lamp curve the wrong way. It should curve AWAY from the straight line, not towards the I-axis. That is because resistance increases, so less current flows than a simple proportion would give.

keyPoints.heading: Required practical — measuring I-V characteristics
keyPoints.content: The required practical asks you to measure I-V characteristics for at least two components. These are usually a resistor and a filament lamp, and sometimes a diode. The circuit uses: - a variable resistor (rheostat) to change the current - an ammeter in series with the component to measure I - a voltmeter in parallel with the component to measure V Record pairs of I and V values as you adjust the variable resistor. Then plot the I-V graph. To get both positive and negative V on the graph, turn the component round. Or swap the battery connections. Safety: filament lamps get very hot, so do not touch the bulb. Keep currents within the given limits so components don't overheat. Always start with the variable resistor at maximum resistance (minimum current) before switching on.
writeBullets: Ammeter — placed in series with the component to measure the current through it
Voltmeter — placed in parallel across the component to measure the p.d. across it
Variable resistor — used to change the current in the circuit and collect many data points
Reverse connections — swap the battery or component to get negative V values and complete the I-V curve
Safety — start at max resistance. The lamp gets very hot. Stay within current limits
Repeats — take repeat readings and average them to reduce random error

keyTerms.def: A resistor whose resistance can be changed — used to vary the current in a circuit
Instrument measuring current; connected in series; has very low resistance
Instrument measuring p.d.; connected in parallel; has very high resistance

keyPoints.memTip: Series A, Parallel V: Ammeter in Series, Voltmeter in Parallel. Cover your notes. Describe the full circuit from memory, including the safety step.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Examiners often ask why each meter goes where it does. The voltmeter is in parallel because it must measure the p.d. across the component. The ammeter is in series to measure the same current that flows through the component. Know the reason, not just the rule.

Fixed resistor in a potential divider

0.question: A charge of 60 C passes through a component in 20 s. What is the current?
0.correctFeedback: Correct. I = Q/t = 60/20 = 3 A. You rearranged Q = It perfectly.
0.wrongFeedback: Rearrange Q = It to I = Q/t. Divide the charge (60 C) by the time (20 s): 60 ÷ 20 = 3 A. Watch out for multiplying instead of dividing, or mixing up the letters.

2.question: A lamp has a p.d. of 12 V across it and a current of 0.5 A through it. What is its resistance at this moment?
2.correctFeedback: Correct. R = V/I = 12 ÷ 0.5 = 24 Ω. Well done for using R = V/I and dividing by a decimal.
2.wrongFeedback: Use R = V/I. Substitute: R = 12 ÷ 0.5 = 24 Ω. Dividing by 0.5 is the same as multiplying by 2, so 12 × 2 = 24 Ω. If you chose 6 Ω, you probably divided by 2 instead of 0.5.

3.question: Which of these best explains why the I-V graph for a filament lamp curves, rather than being straight?
options: The lamp only conducts in one direction
As current increases, the filament heats up, which increases its resistance
The lamp's voltage decreases as current increases
The ammeter reads incorrectly at high currents
3.correctFeedback: Exactly right. The filament heats up and its resistance rises. So the current is lower than a simple proportion would give. That causes the curve.
3.wrongFeedback: The key physics here is temperature. As more current flows, the filament gets hotter. In a metal, a higher temperature means more resistance. The ions vibrate more and block electron flow. So each extra volt gives less extra current than before. That makes the graph curve.

commonMistakes: Drawing the filament lamp I-V curve bending towards the I-axis instead of away from it. It curves away because resistance increases, so less current flows than expected.
Mixing up conventional current and electron flow. Electrons go from − to +. Conventional current goes from + to − in the outside circuit.
Connecting the voltmeter in series instead of parallel. A voltmeter must be in parallel to measure the p.d. across a component without changing the current.
Forgetting to check units in Q = It. Time must be in seconds, not minutes or hours, before substituting.
Saying a diode 'blocks all current' in reverse bias. In reality a tiny reverse current can flow. But at GCSE, its resistance is treated as extremely high.
examTips: Always show the formula, then the substitution, then the answer with units. Even one mark is at stake if you skip a step.

For 'describe and explain' I-V questions, name the shape and then explain the physics. For example: 'The curve means resistance is increasing, because the filament temperature rises as current increases'.
EMF vs terminal p.d.: a question may mention a battery with internal resistance. Then the terminal p.d. is less than the EMF. Say this clearly.

In the required practical, know why each meter goes where it does. Don't just say 'ammeter = series, voltmeter = parallel'. Give the reason. The ammeter measures the current through the component. The voltmeter measures the p.d. across it.
Ohm's law only applies to ohmic conductors at constant temperature. Don't apply it to lamps or diodes without saying so.
revisionCardBullets: Current (I) — the rate of flow of charge. Unit: ampere (A)
Conventional current goes + to −. Electrons flow − to +
Potential difference (V) — energy per unit charge. Unit: volt (V)
EMF — the energy given to each coulomb by the source. Terminal p.d. < EMF
Ohmic conductor — constant resistance. Straight-line I-V graph through the origin
Filament lamp — resistance increases with temperature. Curved I-V graph
Diode — conducts in one direction only. Near-zero current in reverse bias
Ammeter goes in series. Voltmeter goes in parallel
Resistance increases with: greater length, smaller cross-section, higher temperature
